item.title: C++ Language and Library Notes
item.description:
This bounded anthology collects language and toolchain-facing rules that do not require a separate article. Each section states the boundary that governs the feature, because similar-looking C++ spellings can have different ownership, lookup, or lifetime effects.

Resource Ownership and Optional State #

Ownership is the responsibility to release a resource at the correct time. Model it with RAII: acquire in construction, release in destruction, and make the object’s invariant hold across exceptional control flow. Prefer the Rule of Zero when members such as std::unique_ptr or std::vector already implement the resource policy. A type that directly manages a raw resource must define a coherent destructor, copy policy, move policy, and failure policy.

item.title: C++ Declarations, Definitions, and Linkage
item.description:
A declaration introduces a name and describes its type. A definition supplies the entity that the program uses. Linkage determines whether declarations in different scopes or translation units denote the same entity, while storage duration determines how long an object exists. Keeping those four questions separate makes dense C and C++ declarations easier to reason about.

item.title: C++ Copy Elision and Return Values
item.description:
Copy elision permits an implementation to omit copy or move construction even when that constructor or destructor has observable side effects. Before C++17, every elision case was permitted but optional. C++17 changed prvalue semantics, making several former temporary-elision cases direct construction instead.

Returned Prvalues and Named Locals #

Since C++17, a prvalue of the function return type returned from a function constructs the result object directly. A deleted copy and move constructor therefore do not prevent this form, although the returned type’s destructor must still be accessible and non-deleted at the return statement:

item.title: C++ Classes and Special Member Functions
item.description:
A C++ class defines representation, invariants, and the operations that establish and preserve them. Constructors establish an object’s invariant, member functions preserve it, and the destructor releases resources owned by that object. Design the ownership policy first, because it determines whether compiler-generated special members are correct.

Construction and Destruction #

A constructor has the class name and no return type. A default constructor has no parameters or has defaults for all its parameters. Copy and move constructors initialize a new object from an lvalue or rvalue of the same class; copy and move assignment update an existing object.

item.title: C++ Exceptions and Exception Safety
item.description:
Exceptions separate reporting a failed operation from propagating it to a boundary that can respond. An exception transfers control to a matching handler; while control travels outward, C++ destroys every fully constructed automatic object whose scope is exited, in reverse construction order. Resource acquisition is initialization (RAII) therefore makes the normal and exceptional cleanup paths the same.

cpp 
void load_configuration(std::filesystem::path path) {
 std::ifstream input{path}; // Closed during unwinding.
 if (!input) {
 throw std::runtime_error{"cannot open configuration"};
 }
 // Parsing may throw; input still closes.
}

try {
 load_configuration("app.conf");
} catch (const std::exception& error) {
 report(error.what());
}

Throw exception objects by value and catch polymorphic exception types by const reference. Catching a base exception by value slices a derived object. A catch (...) belongs only at a boundary that can restore an invariant, translate an error, or deliberately terminate; it must not silently continue with damaged state.

item.title: C++ Language Rules and Named Requirements
item.description:
C++ language rules determine whether a program is well-formed and what its execution means. Library named requirements and concepts add contracts for generic code. Similar terminology can hide an important distinction: a compiler can check expressions and types, but it cannot prove every semantic, complexity, validity, or equality promise made by a type.

Definitions and the One-Definition Rule #

Every odr-used non-inline function or variable needs one definition in the program. Declarations can be repeated when compatible, which makes forward declarations possible.

item.title: C++ Initialization
item.description: Initialization gives an entity its first value or establishes a reference binding. Assignment changes an object that already exists. Because constructors participate only in initialization and assignment operators participate only after lifetime has begun, the distinction affects overload resolution, invariants, and performance.

item.title: C++ Value Categories and Move Semantics
item.description:
Move semantics are overload selection and type-defined state transfer, not an automatic transfer of ownership. Begin with an expression’s value category, then choose a parameter type that describes ownership and lifetime.

Expression Categories #

Every non-void expression is exactly one of these categories:

  • An lvalue identifies an object, function, or bit-field.
  • An xvalue identifies an object whose resources may be reused.
  • A prvalue computes a value or initializes an object.

Lvalues and xvalues are glvalues; prvalues and xvalues are rvalues. A named variable is an lvalue expression even when it has type T&&.
